title: Into the Void: A Probabalistic Approach to the Search for Missing Aircraft

source.pdf_page_offset_note: Physical pages 1-34 are the formal paper; physical page 35 is a fictional-company stakeholder letter retained as a memo artifact.

notes: All 35 page-text files were read sequentially.
Five bounded overview JPEG proxies covered pages 1-35; fourteen focused formula crops checked pages 5-11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21, and 29.
No blank, clipped, or body-text-overlap page was observed; original PNGs remained coordinate authority.
The page-35 fictional-company letter is categorized as a stakeholder memo, not reference prose.

section_map.summary: The summary states the missing-aircraft decision, prior distribution, four search patterns, Bayesian update, scenario variation, and rectangle recommendation.
The contents makes the route from flight assumptions through probability theory, paths, comparisons, final remarks, and airline letter explicit.
The introduction uses two missing-aircraft incidents to frame time, cost, and survivor-recovery stakes before announcing generic search models.
The nomenclature binds grid, aircraft, detection, path, probability, and effectiveness symbols before equations use them.
The source fixes unpowered flight, one instantaneous turn, no wind/current, floating debris, flat water, runway position, and daylight limits.
Flight geometry and independent descent-angle and bearing distributions construct the initial crash-location probability field.
Bayes theorem updates searched and unsearched grid locations, derives a random-search detection probability, and defines cumulative success.
The continuous probability field becomes a one-square-mile probability grid with explicit range, runway, and daily-search inputs.
Each candidate center is evaluated by usable range, feasible search dimensions, and traversed-grid probability before posterior updating.
A parallel sweep derives square side and path length, then shows five-day posterior maps and twenty-day success curves.
The rectangle generalizes the square area relation and enumerates integer dimensions to improve coverage at greater computational cost.
Spiral geometry derives length-to-side conversion and compares its efficient but less spatially effective route with parallel sweep.
Sector geometry maps path length to an octagon but uses a local center heuristic that the source explicitly calls rudimentary.
Single/multiple aircraft, stall prior, range, mixed paths, and effectiveness variations compare cumulative success under changed scenarios.
The source distinguishes customizability and global square/rectangle optimization from computational cost, sector weakness, assumptions, and absent cost effectiveness.
Future work adds multi-plane pattern optimization, empirical parameters, cost limits, debris dynamics, weather, currents, staging, and refueling.
The conclusion reconnects flight failure, priors, Bayesian updating, paths, scenario tests, and the parallel-sweep recommendation.
References identify incident, flight, search, Bayesian, aircraft, and path sources while leaving frozen data and executable runs absent.
A fictional company letter translates the map, dynamic update, familiar paths, coordinates, and resource claims to commercial-airline readers.

assumptions.summary: The aircraft is tracked until loss, unpowered, in cruise, subject to one instantaneous turn, and modeled without wind, currents, sinking, curvature, land, or non-search transit.
A runway is fixed 400 miles south and each search day has 12 flight hours.
Random-search derivation assumes uniform target distribution, independent uniformly distributed track sections, and no effort outside the region.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Boeing 747-400 example uses L/D 17 and altitude 35,000 feet; values are intended to be replaceable.
Angle standard deviations 15, 20, and 30 degrees are chosen arbitrarily for a likely scenario.
The grid uses one-square-mile cells, square matrix bounds from rmax, and an inscribed circular actual region.
C-130 range, cruise speed, daylight limit, runway distance, and path geometry determine usable search range.

models.summary: Map aircraft glide and bearing assumptions into a crash-location probability field.
Update searched and unsearched probabilities after an unsuccessful sweep.
Derive detection probability from lateral range, path length, and bounded area.
Integrate detection and location mass, then compose day-level success.
Overlay the continuous prior on one-square-mile cells for computation.
Evaluate every grid center using runway range, feasible dimensions, and traversed mass.
Derive a square path from usable distance and maximize swept probability.
Enumerate feasible rectangle dimensions to improve parallel-sweep coverage.
Derive spiral path length and invert it to select a search square.
Map path length to an octagon and optimize a central probability concentration.
Compare paths under aircraft number, stall prior, range, mixed paths, and model geometry.
Scale detection by target visibility and search-aircraft effectiveness.
Bind modular inputs and global square/rectangle optimization to known physical, computational, and economic limits.
Translate model inputs and optimized paths into an audience-facing operational letter.

dependency_graph.handoff: The Cartesian crash prior enters Bayesian cell updates.
Updated cell probabilities enter the detection and random-search model.
Detection probability and posterior mass enter the daily-success objective.
The objective is evaluated on a discrete probability grid.
The grid supplies every candidate center to the daily search optimizer.
Usable range and posterior mass feed square-path evaluation.
Square constraints generalize to enumerated rectangles.
Alternative spiral geometry receives the same daily posterior interface.
Sector geometry receives a bounded central-mass heuristic.
All path outputs enter scenario comparisons.
Effectiveness parameters modify detection in the comparative simulations.
Qualified results and limits inform future operational scope.
The final scope and operations are translated for airline stakeholders.

verification.summary: Five-day posterior and twenty-day curve expose the square model's simulated outputs.
verification.strength: The source displays posterior removal and day-indexed success.
verification.limitation: No empirical incident holdout or calibration is supplied.

verification.summary: Four paths share a cumulative-success comparison.
verification.strength: All paths use the declared simulation interface.
verification.limitation: A common simulated interface does not establish real-world superiority.

verification.summary: A changed pcrash prior reruns all four patterns.
verification.strength: The altered prior and response are displayed.
verification.limitation: The stall weight is not calibrated to incident data.

verification.summary: Unit and doubled effectiveness curves expose nonlinear response.

results_trace.summary: Rectangle leaves fewer gaps than square but costs 20-30 seconds per optimization step versus under one second.
Rectangle is the best single large-plane path; sector is lowest under the displayed simulations.
For short-range aircraft, rectangle leads early but square later outperforms in the stated simulation.
Two squares are preferable to a square-sector pair, but the displayed difference is slight.
The Cessna example has lower visibility but higher modeled success because its search area is smaller.

contributions.summary: Physical glide and bearing uncertainty create a transparent prior rather than a single guessed crash point.
Bayesian updates preserve failed-search probability while renormalizing unsearched locations.
A daily grid optimizer links runway range, geometry, and posterior mass.
Common-scale path curves support conditional geometry selection.
The memo translates technical inputs and outputs to an airline operation.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: The summary binds physical prior, multiple paths, Bayesian update, and operational recommendation without proving that this route caused the award.
A common-scale comparison makes path tradeoffs legible, without validating simulated curves against a real search.
The stakeholder letter reconnects model inputs and outputs to a use case, without proving real deployment readiness.

weaknesses.summary: Coordinate transforms in Equations 6-7 require a dimensional and parenthesis reconstruction before numerical reuse.
Equation 12 visibly omits h from its final fraction and Equation 13 prints h tending to infinity rather than zero in the difference quotient.
Equations 15-16 mix q(z*) and an area integral; the optimization domain and integrand need a typed derivation before implementation.
The printed final simplification in Equation 23 and its inversion in Equation 24 are algebraically unusual and require independent verification.
The sector method explicitly optimizes a product of central mass and usable range rather than the full searched-path success, so it is not a global optimum.
Treating five simultaneous aircraft as one aircraft for five times as many days omits coordination, overlap, and posterior-update timing.
Alpha and beta are hypothetical, multiplicative, and uncalibrated; effectiveness comparisons do not validate their values.
The model omits wind, currents, sinking, curvature, cost effectiveness, and multiple staging constraints central to real deployment.
References do not freeze incident data, distribution calibration, MATLAB code, grid settings, seeds, or reproducible scenario runs.

independent_extensions.summary: Calibrate trajectory mixtures and angle distributions from aircraft-specific incident, weather, and flight-data evidence.
Repair and dimension-check the random-search derivation, then test it against controlled detection trials.
Optimize the full sector path success over all traversed cells rather than a central-mass heuristic.
Use a multi-aircraft, time-indexed, cost-constrained stochastic program with weather, currents, debris state, staging, and sensor models.
